For do not think this alone is the capture of a city, if some, having cast down the wall, slaughter the men and lead away the women and burn the houses; this is perhaps the last and brief and rather prepares the sufferers to be pitied than laughed at; but among those with whom there is neglect of all noble things and a passion for one ignoble matter, and they look to this alone and spend their time about it, leaping and raging and striking one another and saying forbidden things and often reviling the very gods and casting away their possessions and sometimes walking home naked from the spectacle — this is the shameful and reproachful capture of a city.

90. For we say that men have been captured not by robbers only, or by male companions, but also by a courtesan and the belly and some other base desire. He would, then, well be said to have become a captive, both a man and a city, which, having let go the better pursuits and neither seeing nor hearing any of the things that lead to safety, but taken by drunkenness or the song of women or chariots, is led and carried away and is wholly throughout disturbed about this and goes out of its mind; and, by Zeus, he too would be said to have been taken by storm and pinioned who has thus been captured. For if a man's body is mastered and surrounded by certain bonds or guards, one must consider these grievous things captivity and slavery and being led away; but when the soul has been enslaved and ruined, shall we dissemble and make light of it?

91. And yet such things are doubtless dreadful even in individual cases, but altogether more shameful when they appear in public. For the other diseases too, so long as they are among individuals, do not meet with a great or fearful name; but when the thing becomes common, then it is called a plague. For in general one would find all errors everywhere, and there are drunkards and fornicators and woman-mad men in all the cities; but this is not grievous nor extraordinary; but when the passion prevails and is seen as common, then it becomes marked and great and public.

92. For what city is there, of those not very desolate and small, in which someone is not every day at all events feverish? But Caunians alone has it overtaken, and theirs is the reproach, because all of them suffer it; just as from the better things too some men were admired and got repute. For how many of the Athenians or Megarians or Corinthians do you think exercised their bodies and lived laboriously? Many, plainly, and that too when it was necessary for them to become good men on behalf of their fatherlands.

93. Why, then, did the Lacedaemonians alone get this name and enjoy the repute even now? Because they acquired the ambition in common. And the Athenians, practising rather the matters of speech and poetry and choruses, made themselves admired for these by the same cause. Consider, then, lest you partake of a repute not like that of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, but rather of certain others — for I do not wish to name them. For, as I have often said, shameful things are more shameful and more ridiculous when they concern cities.

94. As in the comedies and farces, bringing in Carion drunk and Daos does not greatly move laughter, but to see Heracles such seems ridiculous, carried away and, as they are wont, in a saffron robe; likewise also a people so great droning all its life and again driving without horses becomes shameful and ridiculous. For this very thing Euripides says Heracles suffered when mad: From this point going, having no chariots he said he had them, and mounted the rails of a car, and plied the goad as though he held it in his hand.

95. Do not, then, you too in emulation of Alexander — for he himself said he was a son of Zeus. Or rather perhaps your people resembles not Heracles, but some Centaur or Cyclops who has drunk and is in love, in body strong and great, but in mind untaught. By Zeus, do you not see how great care your emperor has taken of the city? Therefore you too ought to rival him and make your fatherland better — not, by Zeus, with fountains or gateways; for on these you cannot spend, nor would you ever, I think, surpass his magnanimity; but with good order, decorum, by showing yourselves temperate and steadfast. For thus he would neither repent of what has been done and will work you more good. And perhaps you would give him a longing even for his coming hither.

96. For not so much can the beauty of the buildings draw him; for he has all things better and more costly than those anywhere; but when he hears that those who will receive him are worthy of goodwill and trust, and each of those sent and governing you prefers you. For do not think that you inquire about those who sail in, what sort they are, and at once have such an opinion of them as you share of their fame, but that they do not curiously inquire about you, what sort the people of the Alexandrians is. So then, if they hear that it is sensible, but not such as is now said — that it is fluttered, that it is light, admiring the small, mastered by chance matters, a lover of charioteers and citharodes — it is not unclear how they will be disposed.

97. They say that Theophilus, who was a wise man among you, kept silence toward you and would not discourse at all. And yet what opinion do you think he had? Whether that you were wise and needed no treatment? Or rather that he despaired of you as incurable? For it is much as if one of the merchants, having many and precious wares, should sail into a city, then, mastered by certain winds or another fortune and spending a long time there, should neither set out any of his wares nor ever show them; for it is plain that, having judged in them some extreme poverty or inexperience, he would not wish to be troubled in vain, knowing clearly that none of these men would buy nor perhaps even approach.

98. And Theophilus, then, having many and great wares within him there, was conscious of your extreme want, not of money, but of mind and understanding. Therefore he died having kept silence about your city — that is, having condemned it; and you have often heard so-and-so and remember his jests and the songs of so-and-so, but Theophilus I know not if you ever heard; just as one said that the beetles in Attica, the honey being most pure, never taste of it, not even if it be poured out, but of the other food.

99. But you are cheerful and the cleverest of all at jesting. This is not the pursuit of a people — how could it be? — nor of a city, but of some Thersites; for Homer has said that he came among all the Greeks as a buffoon — but because he seemed laughable to the Argives. But the laughable is not good nor precious, but joy; and through want and ignorance of joy men pursue laughter. You have heard, at least, of the herb called sardonion, which produces laughter, but a grievous one and unto destruction.

100. Do not, then, cling so very much to this, nor make the Graces unmusical and vulgar and untaught, but rather imitate Euripides, who speaks thus: May I never cease mingling the Graces with the Muses, sweetest union; that the Museum may not seem to you to be otherwise a place in the city, just as, I think, other places too are named in vain, not having the thing along with the name.

101. But indeed I fear lest there has befallen me too what they say befell one of the Egyptians, a musician of the very ancient ones. For the divine power once foretold to him in sleep that he would sing into an ass's ears. And during all the rest of the time he gave no heed nor thought to the dream, as being nothing. But when the tyrant of the Syrians came to Memphis, the Egyptians, being struck with awe of him, summoned the musician. He displayed, then, with all eagerness even the more exact points of his art; but the tyrant, since he had no understanding of music, bade him stop, dishonouring him. And he, remembering that dream, This, then, he said, was the singing into an ass's ears. And the tyrant, hearing through the interpreters what sort of things he said, beat and scourged the man; and this they say became a cause of war.

1. I wonder what your disposition is, and what you expect or wish when you seek that such men as I should discourse to you. Do you think them sweet-voiced and that they utter more pleasantly than the rest, and then desire to hear them as you would hear birds singing to you? Or that they have another power, in words and thoughts, of a sharper persuasion, and truly formidable, which you call rhetoric, lording it in the marketplaces and about the platform? Or do you think you will hear some praise of yourselves and a public hymn of the city — about Perseus and Heracles and Apollo's trident and the oracles that were given, and how you are Greeks and Argives and even better, and have for your founders heroes and demigods, or rather Titans?

2. And further, I think, about the country and the mountains in it and this Cydnus, how it is the most kindly of all rivers and the fairest, and that those who drink from it are wealthy and blessed according to Homer. For these things are true, and you continually hear them from the poets in verse and from other men who have made this their very work, to eulogize; but it requires great preparation and power.

3. What, then, do you hope we shall say? Or what especially are you eager to hear from men neither witty nor knowing how to converse for favour nor flattering nor coming to their words out of luxury? For that you do not expect money from us nor any other gift I am quite aware. Come, then, let me tell you my own suspicion.

4. You seem to me to have often heard divine men who say they know all things and will speak about all, how they are ordered and what nature they have, both about men and demons and about gods, and further about earth and heaven and sea, and about the sun and moon and the other stars, and about the whole universe, and about destruction and generation and countless other things. Then, I think, coming up to you, they inquire what you wish them to speak about and concerning what — according to Pindar, Ismenus or Melia of the golden distaff or Cadmus; and whatever you think fit, taking thence, he will pour out a full and copious discourse, like some abundant stream shut up within him.

5. Then you, hearing it, think it mean and untimely to examine each point or to disbelieve a wise man, but otherwise you are exalted by the force and speed of the words and rejoice greatly when one strings together so great a crowd of words without taking breath, and you suffer the same as those who watch horses running at full rein; you are not at all benefited, but you marvel nonetheless and call it a blessed possession. And yet even the horses one may see often used not by the masters, but by a mean slave.

6. Such a hearing, then, being a kind of spectacle and procession, has something like the displays of the so-called physicians, who, seating themselves in the midst, go through the junctures of joints and the compositions and juxtapositions of bones and other such things, channels and breaths and filterings. And the many gape and are charmed more than children. But the true physician is not such, nor does he so discourse to those really in need; how could he? But he prescribes what one must do, and forbids the man who wishes to eat or drink, and taking the knife cuts off some part of the body that has mortified.

7. As, then, if the sick, having come together, should make a revel-rout against the physician and think fit to carouse, the matter would not turn out for them according to their hope, but perhaps they would be vexed at the reception; the same thing seems to me to befall the many who come together to such a man and bid him speak, being plainly without taste of the words of truth, and then expecting to hear something sweet and pleasant. Come now, by the gods, will you bear it if one does not use very much frankness nor go through all the things that attach to you, but say only one or two things?

8. Consider, then, lest you suffer the same as those Trojans, who troubled a tragic actor who had come to sojourn, bidding him give a display; but he thought fit to let them be and keep quiet. For by how much, he said, the better I compete, by so much the more unfortunate will you appear. So it is better to let the philosopher keep silent before the many.

9. Consider what the matter is. For the Athenians, being accustomed to hear ill of themselves, and, by Zeus, coming together for this very thing into the theatre, to be reviled, and having set up a contest and victory for those who do it best — not having themselves found this out, but the god having counselled it — used to hear Aristophanes and Cratinus and Plato, and did these no harm. But when Socrates, without stage or scaffolding, performed the god's command, not dancing the kordax nor twittering, they did not endure it.

10. For those men, suspecting and fearing the people as a master, flattered them, biting gently and with laughter, as the nurses do to the children, when they must drink something rather unpleasant, they offer it having smeared the cup with honey. Therefore they harmed no less than they benefited, filling the city with insolence and jests and buffoonery. But the philosopher confuted and admonished.

11. And indeed, how much better it is to revile and to make manifest each man's foolishness and wickedness than to gratify through words and to spoil the hearers with eulogies, you will learn especially from this. For there having been two poets from all time, with whom it is right to compare none of the rest, Homer and Archilochus — of these Homer praised well-nigh everything, both beasts and plants and water and earth and arms and horses, and there is nothing of which he made mention that he passed by without praise and honour, as one might say. The one only of all whom he reviled, Thersites, even him he says was a clear-voiced speaker.

12. But Archilochus came to the opposite, to blame, seeing, I think, that men needed this more, and first he blames himself. Therefore alone, both after his death and before he was born, he obtained the greatest testimony from the divine. For Apollo, driving out of his temple the man who had slain him, declared that he had slain a servant of the Muses. And a second time, when the man made his defense saying he had killed him in war, again Apollo called Archilochus a servant of the Muses. And to his father, consulting the oracle before his birth, the god foretold that an immortal son would be born to him.

13. So that he who is competent to revile and to lay hold and to make manifest by his words men's errors is plainly better and preferred to those who praise. But if indeed you take more pleasure in being praised, you must go to others. Whenever, then, you first see a man flattering himself in all he does and gratifying himself in food, in clothing, and going about licentious, think that this man will flatter you too, and expect from him a sweet discourse, which you call praise — a luxurious man from a luxurious one.

14. But when you see one squalid and contracted and walking alone, examining and reviling himself first, do not seek from such a one any flattery nor deceit, nor that clever and pleasant discourse which especially busies itself about peoples and satraps and tyrants. Not such are the servants of those, but young men, well clad in cloaks and tunics, ever sleek of head and with fair faces. For these come into life like revellers, fluted to and sung to and drunk, thinking they have burst in upon some festival and assembly of prodigals.

15. But whoever, having seen how many grievous and troublesome things there are, and that all is full of foes and enemies where luxury and deceit hold sway, having mastered himself with unseemly blows, casting a bad rag about his shoulders, like a servant, has entered the wide-wayed city of luxurious men — not for any evil of his neighbours, as Odysseus came thus for the evil of the suitors, but on the contrary seeking whether he can do any good unobserved — why do you stir up such a one, or why do you challenge a harsh and savage popular orator, as he will appear to you? For your ears are not prepared to receive rough and hard words; but like the weak hooves of cattle reared in soft and smooth places, so your delicate ears are reared in flattery and false words.

16. Why, then, are you eager to hear what you will not endure? But indeed you have suffered such a thing as Aesop said the eyes suffered, when they thought themselves worth most, but saw the mouth enjoying the other things and indeed the honey, being most sweet. So they were vexed and blamed the man. But when he put some of the honey into them, they were bitten and wept and thought it sharp and unpleasant. Do not, then, you too seek to taste the words from philosophy, as the eyes the honey; for then, I think, being bitten too, you will be displeased and will perhaps say that such a thing is in no way philosophy, but reviling and harm.

17. For you think, men, that you are happy and blessed, since you inhabit a great city and dwell in a good land and see the necessities most abundant and unstinted among you, and this river flows through the middle of your city, and besides Tarsus is the metropolis of those in Cilicia. But Archilochus, who I say pleased Apollo, speaking about a general says thus: I love not a great general nor one straddling wide nor proud of his curls nor close-shaven; but let me have, he says, one bandy-legged, firmly planted, and shaggy on the shins.

18. Do not, then, think that he loved not a general such as he described, and placed the worth of the general not in size of body and a head of hair, but that he would ever praise a city looking to these things — rivers and baths and fountains and porticoes and a multitude of houses and their size; for these resemble simply a head of hair and curls; but it seems to me he would rather choose before these a small and slight one temperately governed, even upon a rock.

19. But Archilochus spoke thus; and Homer, how? Was not Odysseus an islander, and not of the moderate-sized islands? — how could he be? — nor of the fruitful ones, but one which, wishing only to praise it, he called goat-pastured. But nonetheless he says that by this man's counsel and judgment even Troy was taken, so great a city and ruling over so many, as much as Lesbos above, the seat of the blessed, encloses within, and Phrygia above and the boundless Hellespont;

20. which, he says, all called rich in gold, rich in bronze. Did, then, the greatness of their wealth, or the multitude of their subjects or allies, or the plains, or the beauty of Ida, or of the Simois, or of the eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot, profit them at all? And yet he says there were certain very fair springs in the suburb, the one warm and of very gentle water, so that even smoke rose from it, the other like crystal in coldness in summer, so that both in summer and winter the fair daughters of the Trojans washed without difficulty.

21. And they surpassed not only in wealth and in the excellence and extent of the land, but also the fairest of men arose among them, both men and women, and the swiftest horses, and they seemed to be beloved of the gods, and were fenced about with a most strong wall. For their wall was the work of Poseidon and Apollo. And Zeus said that of the cities under the sun he loved that one most. The swiftness of horses was such that they ran upon the tops of the ears of corn. And for beauty Zeus made Ganymede his cup-bearer. And after Alexander there followed from Greece the best of the women there. And Homer says that Cassandra fell not short of Aphrodite in form.

22. But nonetheless, when luxury and insolence entered into them and they thought they needed nothing of education and temperance, they became by far the most unfortunate of all. Is not the whole earth full of the report of their misfortunes? And nothing profited them, neither the swiftness of horses nor Zeus nor Ganymede, but by a man from so sorry and obscure a city they perished, and the citizen of Ithaca prevailed to overcome all those from Ilium, and to sack and destroy the whole wide-wayed city.

23. For not even do the gods any longer love the wanton and senseless and licentious and those inclined to insolence and idleness and luxury. So do not take courage in these things, nor accept the discourse that rejoices with you and admires you, nor those clever at eulogizing; for these deceive you and exalt you in vain, as silly children; but rather him who will show you some of your errors and, first of all, if he can, will make you understand that, on account of these things which I have mentioned, you are not happy — not even if the Nile flowed through your city become clearer than Castalia, nor if Pactolus, appearing here, brought you gold not in grains, as they say it did to the Lydians of old, but in a mass like mud, nor if you surpass Egypt or Babylon in the costliness of your buildings.

24. For if these things can make men blessed — a river or temper of air or place of earth or harbours of the sea or a temple or a wall — it is not possible to say in how many things you are deficient. You hear of those Byzantines who dwell on the very Pontus, a little outside the mouth, fish sometimes falling out upon the land of themselves; but nonetheless no one would say the Byzantines were happy on account of the fish, unless the gulls too, nor the Egyptians on account of the Nile, nor the Babylonians on account of the wall.

25. Does not the Peneus flow through a desolate Thessaly? Does not the Ladon through an Arcadia laid waste? Is not the Cydnus itself purer above? What then? Will you on this account say those people are better than yourselves? Perhaps you speak truly, if you say it; yet you will not say it. For those without trial of luxury and villainy — these, I say, fare better. And what of Italy itself? Did not Sybaris, by how much most it lived luxuriously, by so much the more quickly perish? And Croton and Thurii and Metapontum and Tarentum, having flourished to so great a height and once had so great power, of what city are they not now more desolate?

26. It would be much work to go through all who have perished through luxury — the Lydians of old, the Medes, the Assyrians before them, last of all the Macedonians; who, lately stripped of their rags and called shepherds and fighting with the Thracians about the millet-fields, mastered the Greeks, crossed into Asia, ruled as far as the Indians. But when they took the good things of the Persians, the evils too followed upon these.

27. Therefore at once sceptres and purple robes and the Median table and their race failed; so that now, if one should pass through Pella, he will see no sign of a city at all, except that there is much broken pottery in the place. And yet the sites of the cities I have mentioned remain, and of the nations, such as they were before, and no one has turned the rivers elsewhere, nor if there was any other such thing; but nonetheless, whatever costliness and luxury have laid hold of, for these it is not possible to last a longer time.

28. For do not think that the rams nor the siege-engines nor the other machines so overturn as luxury, whether one wishes to see a man fallen or a city. It is not a river nor a plain nor a harbour that makes a city happy, nor a multitude of money nor of buildings nor treasures of the gods, to which the divine pays no heed; nor if some transfer the mountains and the rocks into the cities with much toil and labour and countless expense; but temperance and mind are the things that save. These make those who use them blessed, these make them dear to the gods, not frankincense nor myrrh — how could it? — nor roots and tears of trees nor the brushwood of the Indians and Arabs.

29. But you, if by chance the river changes and flows muddier, are vexed and lay the blame on those who first sojourned among you; but seeing the character of the city changing and becoming worse and ever more disturbed, you take no thought. But you wish water not only to drink pure, but also to look on;

30. yet a pure and moderate character you do not seek. And yet one may often hear some say: For have we alone changed, and not well-nigh all? But this is as if someone in a plague, because all or most are sick, should wish to take no forethought to be himself in health; or, by Zeus, being storm-tossed at sea, then seeing all in the ship in danger, should neglect his own safety. What? If the whole fleet sink, is what happens on this account less strange?

31. What, then, do we err in? The rest I leave aside. For it is ridiculous if one should attempt to tell a man who does not know at all how to play the lyre, but strums at random, what he erred in or what note he passed over. But this much only is worth saying, which no one would deny. I say, then, that a marvellous experience has befallen many in this city, which I formerly heard occurred among certain others rather than among you.

32. But what this is, if I cannot make plain clearly, do you yourselves try to suspect; and do not think I speak any of the unspeakable things, nor what those who do them conceal, even if it seem very marvellous. In the very midst, at least, walking upright, talking, the most are asleep; but if to the most they seem to be awake, this would be nothing. For one of the inexperienced will say the hares are awake, if he see them sleeping. Whence, then, was this known? From certain other things, which are signs of sleeping; since their eyes are open.

33. What, then, do these do, being asleep? Many other things; for well-nigh all their deeds resemble dreams. For they rejoice in vain and grieve and are bold and afraid, there being nothing, and are eager, and desire impossible things, and think things that are not to be, and do not perceive the things that are. Except that these are perhaps common to us too. But that, I think, is the plainest proof of sleep that they give — they snore. For I cannot, by the gods, say it more decently. And yet of those asleep too few ever suffer this; but of the rest it befalls the drunken and the gorged and those lying ill.

34. But I say that this deed makes the city shameful and disgraces it publicly, and that those who sleep thus by day outrage their fatherland with the greatest insolence, and that they would justly be banished both from you and from everywhere. For what happens is not moderate nor rarely occurring, but always and everywhere in the city, even if one threaten, even if one jest, even if one laugh. And henceforth it is now habitual even to the very small children, and of the grown men those who seem to be modest are often led on to use it as upon some gift, and even if, checking themselves, they are abashed, they at all events breathed out the like.

35. If, then, there were such a city that one ever heard people lamenting in it, and no one could go forth even for a little without this ill-omened sound, by Zeus, is there anyone who would gladly sojourn there? And yet lamenting, as one might say, is a sign of misfortune, but such a thing of shamelessness, of the utmost wantonness. Reasonably, then, one would wish to spend time among unfortunate men rather than among licentious. For I, for my part, would not choose to hear even flute-players continually; but if there is such a place, in which there is a continual sound either of flutes or of song or of the lyre, such as they say the crag of the Sirens is, ever sung over, I could not, having gone there, pass my time.

36. But this savage and grievous sound, what moderate man would endure? But if one, passing a house, hear such a thing, plainly he will say it is a brothel. But what will they call the city, in which everywhere well-nigh one sound prevails, and they make no time nor day nor place exempt, but in the alleys, in the houses, in the marketplaces, beside the theatre, in the gymnasium the thing holds sway? And of anyone playing the flute at dawn I have heard none up to now in the city, but this marvellous melody is set in motion straightway with the day.

37. And yet it has not escaped me that perhaps some think me trifling in examining such things, and that there is nothing besides this, only that you bring in vegetables by the wagonload and behold many loaves in the midst and there is salt-fish and meat. Yet let them consider the matter thus themselves. If one of them should come to a city in which all, whatever they point at, point with the middle finger, and if one give the right hand, gives it thus, and if one stretch out the hand thus, and if the people vote, and if the jurors cast their ballot, what sort of city will they consider this? And if all walk with their garments tucked up, as in a marsh?

38. Are you ignorant that these are the things that have given an occasion against you for slander, so that those ill disposed toward you have, against the city publicly, something to say? But why do they cry out the weaving-shuttles at you? And yet they say it ought to make no difference, either to you or to others, about what others say, but about what you yourselves do. Come, if such an affliction should overtake some publicly, that all take the voice of women, and no one, neither young nor old, can say anything in a manly way — will it not seem grievous and, I think, heavier than any plague? For it is not shameful to be feverish nor to die; so that they would send to the god and propitiate the divine much. And yet for women to utter a woman's voice is to utter a human voice, and no one hearing a woman would be displeased.

39. But such a sound, of whom is it? Is it not of the androgynous? Is it not of those whose privy parts have been cut off? And not even of these always and toward all, but it is peculiar to them as a kind of token. Come, suppose you all walked girt up or beating drums, and this seemed to you nothing grievous? If it befell you to have some lofty height or, by Zeus, an overhanging mountain, as other cities, where one who has gone up cannot hear each clearly, but the whole din, what sort of sound do you think would be borne up to you? Or is it plain that the greater part prevails as in harmony?

40. But if one must judge about men from the hearing — as Homer says that Odysseus, approaching his own house, did not wait to see the suitors feasting, but straightway said to Eumaeus, as the lyre carried round to him, that he knew many were holding a feast in it;

41. and again, from the island of the Cyclopes, hearing both the sheep bleating and their voice, as of men, I think, pasturing, that he understood the country was of certain shepherds — come, if one should conjecture about you too from the sound borne afar, what sort of men would he suppose you to be and to be doing what? For you are not competent either to herd cattle or to tend sheep; and which will one say — that you are colonists of the Argives, as you say, or rather of those Aradians? And which — Greeks or the most licentious of the Phoenicians? For I think it rather befits a temperate man in such a city to smear his ears with wax than if he happened to be sailing past the Sirens. For there there was a danger of death, but here of wantonness, of insolence, of the utmost corruption.

42. And there is no pleasure besides, nor instruction, I suppose. Formerly, then, the exhortation of the better prevailed, but now, as it seems, that of the worse. And one might wonder at the cause of the more here emulating it and its ever becoming more habitual as it advances. As a certain Ionian mode prevailed, and a Dorian and another Phrygian and a Lydian, so now the music of the Aradians prevails, and the strummings of the Phoenicians please you, and you have especially loved this rhythm, as others the spondaic;

43. or has a race of men appeared musical in the nostrils, as they say the swans are in their wings, and then, in the manner of clear-voiced birds, they delight one another both in the streets and at banquets, needing neither lyre nor flutes — for these are old-fashioned instruments of some still harsh and rustic music — but now another mode flourishes, better and more pleasant than lyres? So then, after a time, we shall set up choruses of boys and maidens under this melody, having carefully taught them.

44. But that you are vexed hearing this I know clearly, and I foretold that you would receive the words not gladly. But you perhaps thought I would discourse about stars and earth. And some of you are angry and say I outrage the city, but do not blame those who do these things; and some perhaps laugh, if I found nothing better to speak about. But I see that the physicians too sometimes touch what they would not wish, not the fairest parts of the body, and I know that many of those being treated are indignant when one touches the afflicted part. But he often scratches it and cuts while the man cries out. So I will not cease speaking about this until you are greatly bitten. And yet you meet with this discourse as a very weak drug and much less than according to your desert.

45. Come now, by Heracles and Perseus and Apollo and Athena and the other gods whom you honour, answer me eagerly: if any of you wished to have such a wife — I mean, as a woman is called a lyre-player, and, by Zeus, a flute-player or poetess and the rest likewise from their other pursuits, so one whom one would customarily name from this practice. And be not displeased nor vexed; for the matter itself furnishes these words to one who wishes to speak about it, not I who find them from somewhere. To live with such a woman, then, none of you would wish, not even for five hundred talents, I think; but would one choose to have such a daughter? But, by Zeus, somehow it is not grievous to have such a mother and to support her in old age; for it is plainly august and more befitting elder women.

46. Well; so in the case of a wife or a daughter you do not even endure to hear of it, but to dwell in such a city and fatherland does not seem dreadful to you? And that too — which is altogether more grievous — not being such from the beginning, but such as you yourselves make it. And yet your city is a metropolis, so that it has both the augustness and the dignity of a mother; but nonetheless you spare neither the name nor the antiquity nor the repute.

47. What, then, do you think, if, as is likely and as they say, the founder heroes or gods often turn their attention to their own cities, being unseen to the rest, at sacrifices and certain public festivals — then your founder Heracles should be present, whether at a pyre, which you make very fine for him — would he be greatly pleased hearing such a sound? Would he not rather go off to Thrace or Libya and be present with the descendants of Busiris or Diomedes when they sacrifice? And what? Does not Perseus seem really to fly over the city? And what need to mention gods?

48. But Athenodorus, who was lately among you, whom Augustus respected — do you think, if he had known the city to be such, he would have preferred his sojourn here to that with him? Formerly, then, your city was renowned for good order and temperance and produced such men; but now I fear lest it take the opposite rank, so that it be named along with these and those. And yet many of the things still remaining somehow display the temperance and the austerity of the upbringing of that time, among which is the matter concerning the dress of the women, their being arranged in this manner and walking so that no one may see any one part of them, neither of the face nor of the rest of the body, nor that they themselves see anything off the road.

49. And yet what can they see such as they hear? Therefore, beginning the corruption from the ears, the most have perished. For wantonness creeps in from every side, both through ears and through eyes. So that they walk with their faces covered, but with the soul uncovered and very wide open. Therefore they see more keenly with one of their eyes, like the geometers.

50. And this matter of the nostrils is conspicuous. But the rest too must follow such a rhythm. For do not think that, as on others some local disease often falls upon certain parts, hands or feet or face, so among you too a local disease has fallen upon the nostrils, nor, as they say Aphrodite in anger corrupted the armpits of the Lemnian women, here too suppose that the nostrils of the most have been corrupted by divine wrath, and then they utter such a voice; how could that be? But it is a sign of the utmost insolence and madness and of despising all noble things and considering nothing shameful.

51. I say, then, that they converse like these and walk and look. But if they cannot make anything so conspicuous through their glances as to turn all heads, or have not yet advanced the art so far, in nothing else are they more decent. Then you are vexed with the Aegeans and the Adanians when they revile you, but do you not banish from the city those of your own citizens who bear witness to those people that they speak truly?

52. Do you not know that to do any of the unspeakable and unnatural things has in most cases only suspicion, and no one has seen any of the many, but somewhere in the dark and secretly the wretches commit impiety undetected; but such tokens of incontinence betray the character and the disposition — the voice, the look, the bearing, and indeed these things that seem small and of no account, the haircut, the gait, the rolling of the eyes, the inclining of the neck, the conversing with the hands upturned? For do not think that flute-tunes and strummings and melodies, some show the manly, others the womanish, but that movements and actions make no difference nor are any proof in these. But I wish to tell you a story which perhaps you have heard at another time too.

53. They say that one of the clever men here came to a certain city having made this his very work, so as to know at once each man's character and to describe his attributes, and to fail in nothing at all; but, as we know animals by seeing, that this is a sheep, if it so be, and this a dog, and this a horse or ox, so that man knew men by seeing and could say that this one is brave, this one cowardly, this one a braggart, this one insolent or lewd or an adulterer.

54. As, then, he was marvellous in his displays and nowhere failed, they bring to him a man hard of body and with brows knit, squalid and meanly disposed and having calluses on his hands, wrapped in some grey and rough garment, hairy down to the ankles and meanly shorn; and they thought fit for him to say who he was. And he, as he looked a long time, at last, hesitating, it seems to me, to say what occurred to him, said he did not understand, and bade him walk. And as he was now departing, he sneezes; and that man straightway cried out that he was lewd.

55. Then in the case of a man the sneeze convicted his character and prevailed against all else not to escape notice; but shall not one such thing slander a city and fill it with bad repute, and that too where it needs no clever one to understand of what it is a sign? But I, for my part, would gladly inquire of the experienced what this resembles or what it means to show. For it is neither a clucking nor a clicking nor a whistling; or of what work is it proper and when especially does it occur; for they do not pasture thus nor plough nor hunt, nor is it the voice of sailors.

56. Is it, then, of those greeting one another or calling or being friendly? But, as the wedding-song is some peculiar ancient melody for those marrying, so this new rhythm has been invented of some other festival. But you will depart vexed and saying I have trifled, if I have arranged so many words in vain and toward none of the useful things. For no harm comes from this, you say, nor is the city worse governed.

57. But among the Greeks formerly it seemed a dreadful thing to change the music, and all cried out against those who introduced another rhythm and made the melodies more elaborate, as though Greece were being corrupted in the theatres. So very much did they guard their ears and thought the hearing had so great a power as to make the mind effeminate and to wrong temperance, if the matter of harmony yielded a little. Therefore they say that the Lacedaemonians, when Timotheus came to them, being now brilliant and dominant in music, both took away his lyre and cut out the superfluous of the strings. And you too, men of Tarsus, imitate the Lacedaemonians, cut out the superfluous sound.

58. The old myth says that Circe changed men with her drugs, so that swine and wolves came to be from men; and these things we disbelieve when Homer says them: They had the heads of swine and the voice and bristles and shape. But of those he says the mind remained steadfast, but of these the mind has first perished and been corrupted.

59. And indeed it is not so dreadful if men in the midst should take the voice of sheep or of cattle, nor if they neigh nor if they bark, as the poets say of Hecuba, that at last, after all the dreadful things, the Erinyes made her a fierce-eyed dog, and uttering bronze sounds from her grey jaws there harkened Ida and sea-girt Tenedos and the Thracian wind-loving fields.

60. I say this is not so dreadful a portent nor so abominable as when a man, being a man and having the same character and his own voice, and being unable to abolish the signs of his nature, not even if he do everything in concealing them, like a thief his stolen goods, being struck by certain Erinyes and twisted and broken in every way, wishes to do everything, and nothing as it is by nature; and then, in the manner of some Proteus, changing and altering himself, finds a way to utter a voice neither of a man nor of a woman nor of any other animal, imitating a foul and androgynous creature, nor like a harlot who does this very thing harlotting, but as though uttering the very sound of the most shameful work and the most licentious act, and that too by day, when the sun is conspicuous, with many present. It was not so dreadful that the hides of the cattle crept nor that the meat bellowed.

61. What Homer, then, or what Archilochus is strong enough to sing away these evils? For to me, by Heracles, the matter of men seems to need some noble and tragic poet, who will be able to check and beat back so great a rush;

62. since now what happens resembles a shameful and unseemly madness, and this disease of unseemliness and shamelessness, going round in a circle, leads you henceforth to everything, both deeds and voices and bearings, and lays hold of and reaches every part — feet, hands, eyes, tongue. So there is no use in us nor in this slack and weak exhortation, but rather there is need of some Stentor uttering a bronze or iron voice, who will shout louder and clearer than I. For you see whither it advances.

63. The trimming of the beard was first found, and this seemed moderate, the not letting it down too much, nor too long, but gently amending nature. So such a man seemed to many clever. Then they shaved as far as the cheeks; not even this yet dreadful; but nonetheless the comic poet bade even this man be burned upon sixteen fig-wood phalluses. Except that they had comely faces and boyish beyond their age, freed from this down; then, what was still left, the legs and the breast, that we may in the rest too be like boys. Then as far as the arms; then passing to the privy parts, where puberty too seems superfluous, the art of nature is mocked and laughed at by the wise and the young, as being something old-fashioned and very silly, having added useless and superfluous things to the body.

64. For what need had you of nails, what of hair? But neither perhaps of hands nor feet. You needed only to make privy parts and bellies and to set food beside them and the other things which one can enjoy. Therefore we ourselves clip ourselves, and take away the beard and the puberty, which are peculiar to men; but if it were possible to add the other things from the women, plainly we should then be altogether happy, not, as now, being deficient, but whole and androgynous according to nature.

1. I happened to be sojourning in Borysthenes in the summer, when I had sailed in after my exile, wishing to go, if I could, through the Scythians to the Getae, that I might observe what the affairs there were like. And so I was walking about toward the time when the market is full, beside the Hypanis. For the city has taken its name from the Borysthenes, because of the beauty and greatness of the river, but it lies near the Hypanis, both the present city and the one formerly so inhabited, not far above the so-called promontory of Hippolaus, on the opposite side.

2. This is a sharp and firm point of the land like a beak, about which the rivers meet. And from there on already they form a marsh as far as the sea for nearly two hundred stades; and the breadth there is not less than that of the rivers. And the greater part of it is shallow, and a calm forms in fair weather, steady as in a lake. But on the right a river appears, and those sailing in conjecture the depth from the current. Whence indeed it also flows out, through the strength of the stream; otherwise it would easily be blocked when the south wind blows strongly in against the mouth.

3. The rest is a marshy shore, thick with reed and trees. And many of the trees appear even in the midst of the marsh, so as to resemble masts, and ere now some of the more inexperienced went astray, taking them for boats. And here too is the abundance of the salt, whence the most of the barbarians get it, buying the salt, both of the Greeks and of the Scythians those who dwell on the Tauric Chersonese. And the rivers empty into the sea by the fort of Alector, which is said to belong to the wife of the king of the Sauromatae.

4. But the city of the Borysthenites is not in greatness up to its ancient repute, because of the continual captures and the wars. For, dwelling so long a time now in the midst of the barbarians, and these well-nigh the most warlike, it is ever warred upon, and has often been taken; and the last and greatest capture was not more than a hundred and fifty years ago. And the Getae took this too and the other cities on the left of the Pontus as far as Apollonia.

5. Whence indeed the affairs of the Greeks there became very lowly, some of the cities being no longer settled together, others meanly, and the most of the barbarians flowing together into them. For many captures have occurred in many parts of Greece, scattered as it is in many places. And the Borysthenites, having then been captured, settled again, with the Scythians willing it, I think, because of their needing the trade and the resort of the Greeks. For they ceased sailing in when the city was made desolate, having none of the same speech to receive them, nor did the Scythians think fit, nor know how, to furnish them a trading-post in the Greek manner.

6. And a sign of the desolation is the meanness of the buildings and the contraction of the city into a small compass. For it has been built up against a certain part of the ancient circuit, where some few towers remain, not in keeping with the greatness or the strength of the city. And the space between is filled in along that part with the houses not leaving any gaps. And a wall is laid alongside, very low and weak. And of the towers there are some far distant from the part now inhabited, so that one could not even conjecture they belonged to one city. These, then, are clear signs of the capture, and the fact that none of the statues in the temples remains sound, but all are mutilated, like those on the tombs.

7. As, then, I said, I happened to be walking before the city, and some of the Borysthenites came out to me from within, as they were wont; then Callistratus, on horseback, at first rode past us, driving up from outside, but going a little ahead got down, and handing his horse to his attendant, himself approached very decorously, having drawn his hand under his cloak. He was girt with a great sword of the cavalry kind, and wore trousers and the rest of the Scythian dress, and above on his shoulders a small black cloak, thin, as the Borysthenites are wont. They use also other clothing for the most part black, from a certain race of the Scythians, the Melanchlaeni — so named, it seems to me, by the Greeks on this account.

8. And Callistratus was about eighteen years old, very fair and tall, having much of the Ionian in his look. And he was said to be brave too in matters of war, and to have slain many of the Sauromatae and taken others captive. And he was zealous also about speeches and philosophy, so that he even desired to sail away with me. For all these things he was of good repute among the citizens, and not least from his beauty, and he had many lovers. For this has very much remained among them from the mother-city, the love of males; so that they run the risk of persuading some of the barbarians too, not for good, I think, but as those would receive such a thing, in barbarian fashion and not without insolence.

9. Knowing, then, that he was a lover of Homer, I straightway inquired about this. And well-nigh all the Borysthenites are zealous about the poet, perhaps because they are still warlike now, unless indeed it is also because of their goodwill toward Achilles; for they honour this man exceedingly, and have established a temple to him on the island called Achilles' island, and another in the city; so that they will not even hear of anyone else than Homer. And in other respects no longer clearly speaking Greek, through dwelling in the midst of the barbarians, nonetheless well-nigh all of them know the Iliad by heart.

10. I said, then, playfully to him: Which seems to you, Callistratus, the better poet, Homer or Phocylides? And he, laughing, said: But I, for my part, do not even know the other poet's name, nor, I think, does any of these. For we consider no other poet than Homer. But him well-nigh no one else is ignorant of. For of Homer alone their poets make mention in their poems, and otherwise too they are wont to recite him, but always whenever they are about to fight they exhort their own men, just as the verses of Tyrtaeus were recited in Lacedaemon. And these are all blind, and do not think it possible for anyone to become otherwise a poet.

11. This, I said, their poets have got from Homer as from an ophthalmia. But Phocylides you do not know, as you say; yet he has been of the very famous poets. As, then, whenever one of the merchants sails in to you not having come before, you do not straightway dishonour him, but first having tasted the wine, and if he bring some other cargo, having taken a sample, if it please you, you buy, but if not, you let it be; so, I said, of the poetry of Phocylides too it is possible for you to take a sample in brief. For he is not one of those who string together a long and continuous poem,

12. as your poet goes through one battle in succession in more than five thousand verses, but by twos and threes of verses his poetry both takes a beginning and an end. So that he even adds his name to each thought, as considering it serious and worth much, not as Homer nowhere in his poetry named himself.

13. Or does it not seem to you that Phocylides reasonably added to such a maxim and declaration this too: And this is of Phocylides: a small city dwelling in order upon a crag is stronger than senseless Nineveh. But are not these verses, for those who hear not carelessly, worth a whole Iliad and Odyssey? Or was it more profitable to you to hear about the leapings and rushings of Achilles, and his voice, that merely by uttering it he routed the Trojans — does this profit you more to learn thoroughly, than that the small city lying on a rough crag is stronger and more fortunate dwelling in order than a great one in a smooth and broad plain, if indeed it be inhabited disorderly and lawlessly by senseless men?

14. And he, not very gladly accepting it, said: O stranger, it is because we love you and respect you greatly; since otherwise none of the Borysthenites would have endured one saying such things against Homer and Achilles. For the one is our god, as you see, and the other is honoured well-nigh next after the gods. And I, wishing to soothe him, and at the same time to lead him to something useful, said: I beg you, according to Homer, to grant me pardon, "if anything ill has now been said." For at another time we shall praise Achilles and Homer in whatever they seem to us to speak rightly.

15. But the present matter would be the saying of Phocylides; for to me he seems to speak very nobly about the city. Consider it, he said, since you see all these too desiring to hear you and for this reason having flowed together hither to the river, although they are not very free from disturbance. For you know, doubtless, that yesterday the Scythians, driving up at midday, killed some of the scouts who were not attending, and have perhaps taken others alive; for we do not yet know, because their flight became longer for them, since they fled not toward the city.

16. And this was really so, and the gates had been shut and the war-signal had been raised on the wall. But nonetheless they were so fond of listening and Greek in character, that well-nigh all were present in arms, wishing to hear. And I, admiring their eagerness, said: Would you wish that we sit down, going somewhere in the city? For perhaps now not all hear alike while walking, but those behind have trouble and give trouble to those before them, hastening to come nearer.

17. As I said this, they all straightway rushed to the temple of Zeus, where they are wont to deliberate. And the eldest and the most notable and those in the offices sat round on benches; but the rest of the multitude stood by. For there was much open space before the temple. A philosopher would have been very pleased at the sight, that all were after the ancient manner, as Homer says of the Greeks, wearing long hair and having let their beards grow, and one only among them shaven, and him all reviled and hated. And it was said that he practised this for no other reason than flattering the Romans and displaying his friendship toward them; so that one might see in his case the shamefulness of the thing and in no way befitting men.

18. When there was quiet, I said that they seemed to me to do rightly, dwelling in an ancient and Greek city, in wishing to hear about a city. And first, I said, one must clearly know this very thing about which the discourse is; for thus you would at once also have perceived what sort of thing it is. For the many men, I said, know the very name and utter it of each thing, but are ignorant of the thing.

19. But the educated take care of this, that they shall know also the meaning of each thing of which they speak; for instance, the name of "man" all who speak Greek so utter, but if you ask one of them what this is — I mean what sort of thing and in what it is the same as nothing else — he could not say, but only point at himself or another, like the barbarians. But the experienced answers him who asks what man is, that he is a rational mortal animal. For to be this has befallen man alone and no other.

20. So, then, they say the city too is a multitude of men dwelling in the same place governed by law. It is now plain, then, that this appellation befits none of the so-called cities that are senseless and lawless. So neither would the poet have spoken of Nineveh as of a city, since it was senseless. For just as that is not a man to whom the rational is not present, so neither is that a city to which it has not fallen to be lawful. And it would never be lawful, being senseless and disorderly.

21. Perhaps, then, one might inquire whether, when the rulers and those in authority are prudent and wise, but the rest of the multitude is governed according to their judgment lawfully and temperately, one ought to call such a one temperate and lawful and truly a city, from those who govern it; as we should call a chorus musical, perhaps, the leader being musical, the rest following him and uttering nothing out of tune, or but little and indistinctly.

22. For a city good out of all good men no one knows ever to have arisen as mortal before, nor is it worth conceiving as ever going to be hereafter — save the city of the blessed gods in heaven, in no way unmoved nor idle, but vigorous and moving, the gods who lead and are first being without strife and defeat; for it is not lawful for gods either to strive or to be defeated, neither by one another, being friends, nor by others stronger, but to do their own works unhindered with all friendship ever common to all; the most conspicuous proceeding each by himself, not wandering otherwise a senseless wandering, but dancing a blessed dance with mind and the highest prudence; and the rest of the multitude being led by the common movement with one judgment and impulse of the whole heaven.

23. For this one constitution, or city if one must so call it, is purely happy — the communion of the gods with one another — even if one include also the whole rational, men being reckoned with the gods, as children are said to share in the city with men, being citizens by nature, not by thinking and doing the things of citizens nor by sharing in the law, being without understanding of it. But out of the others everywhere, well-nigh simply all erring and mean toward the highest straightness of the divine and blessed law and the right governance, nonetheless for the present we shall be well off for an example of the one more reasonably disposed compared with the one altogether corrupt, as among all the sick we compare the one faring most lightly with the one in the worst case.

24. I, then, was setting out in my discourse toward some such thing. But in the midst one of those present uttered into the open, who was the eldest of them and had the greatest dignity, and said very cautiously: By no means, stranger, consider it rustic or barbarian, that I have stood in your way while you were speaking in the midst. For among you it is not a custom because of the great abundance of words from philosophy and because it is possible to hear from many about everything one may desire; but among us it has appeared like some marvel, this coming of you to us.

25. For the rest, well-nigh, come hither Greeks in name, but in truth more barbarous than we, merchants and hucksters, bringing in mean rags and bad wine and taking out the things from us no better than these. But Achilles himself seems to have sent you hither to us from the island, and we both see you very gladly and very gladly hear whatever you may say. Yet we do not think this will be for any long time, nor do we wish it, but that, having fared well, you may return home as quickly as possible.

26. Now, then, since you have touched in your discourse on the divine governance, I myself have been marvellously winged, and I see all these eager for that discourse; for to us you seemed to have said all you said magnificently and not unworthily of the matter, and as we should most wish to hear. For of this more exact philosophy we are inexperienced, but lovers of Homer, as you know, and certain few of Plato; of whom you see I too am one, ever meeting with his works as far as I can; and yet it is perhaps strange that one who speaks barbarously should most of the citizens delight in and consort with the most Greek and wisest, just as if one well-nigh blind should turn away from all other light, but look up at the very sun.

27. So our affairs stand thus. But if you are willing to gratify us all, put off the discourse about the mortal city — if indeed the neighbours grant us leisure for tomorrow and there be no need to exercise against them, as is our wont for the most part; but about the divine, whether you please to call it a city or an ordering, tell where and how it stands, drawing as near as you can to Plato's freedom of expression, such indeed as you seemed to us just now to do. For if of nothing else, of the voice at least we understand through habit that it utters nothing small nor far from Homer.

28. And I was greatly pleased at the simplicity of the old man, and laughing said: O dear Hieroson, if you had bidden me yesterday, when the enemy had broken in upon you, take arms like Achilles and fight, the one thing I should have been persuaded to, trying to defend friendly men, but the other I think I could not have done, though greatly wishing it, to fight like Achilles. And now, of the things you bid, I will do the one, I will eagerly try to speak the discourse as I can by myself; but with men before me I shall not be willing to strive, neither with Plato nor with Homer. For not even to Eurytus, the poet says, did it profit that he strove against his betters. Yet of zeal, I said, we shall leave nothing out.

29. Having said this to him, I was nonetheless stirred and borne up in a manner, having recalled both Plato and Homer. The matter of the city, then, I said, one must so hear, as that our people do not directly declare the universe a city; for this would be contrary to the argument about the city, which, as I said, they defined as a system of men; and at the same time it was perhaps not fitting nor convincing, having properly said the universe is a living being, then to assert that it is a city;

30. for the same thing, both a city and a living being, no one, I think, would readily endure to suppose. But the present ordering, when the whole has been divided and parted into many forms of plants and of mortal and immortal animals, and besides of air and earth and water and fire, being nonetheless one by nature in all these and governed by one soul and power, they somehow liken to a city, because of the multitude of those who come into being and pass away in it, and besides the order and the good arrangement of the governance.

31. And this argument has been earnest, in brief, to fit the human race to the divine, and to comprehend in one principle all the rational, finding this alone the strong and indissoluble origin of fellowship and justice. For a city would on this account be so called, by Zeus, not having met with mean nor small leaders, nor torn apart and in faction all the time by tyrants and democracies and decarchies and oligarchies and certain other such infirmities, but adorned with the most temperate and best kingship, really ruled by a king according to law with all friendship and concord;

32. which indeed the wisest and eldest ruler and lawgiver ordains to all, mortals and immortals, the leader of the whole heaven and the master of all being, himself thus expounding and furnishing as an example his own governance of the happy and blessed condition; whom the divine poets, having learned from the Muses, hymn and at the same time name father of gods and men.

33. For the poetic race runs the risk, after all, of being not altogether wide of the sacred discourses, nor of uttering such things often off the mark; yet neither of having been purely initiated according to ordinance and law of those initiated, nor of knowing anything clear about the truth concerning the universe, so to speak; but it simply resembles those servants of the rites outside about the doors, who adorn the porches and the altars in the open and prepare the other such things, but never go inside. Whence indeed they name themselves servants of the Muses, not initiates nor any other august name.

34. So then, as I said, those who move about near some rite at the entrances are likely to perceive at least so much of what is within, either some single mystic word shouted out or fire appearing above; and to the poets sometimes — I mean the very ancient ones — a short voice from the Muses came, and somewhere some inspiration of the divine nature and of truth, like a gleam of fire shining from the unseen; which things Homer and Hesiod experienced from the Muses and were possessed by.

35. But those after them later, having brought their wisdom to stages and theatres, uninitiated themselves often brought forth to the uninitiated imperfect examples of the mysteries; and being admired by the many they attempted themselves to initiate the crowd, having really set up some uncovered Bacchic stages at certain tragic crossroads. But all these poets alike call the first and greatest god father, in sum, of the whole rational race, and indeed king too.

36. Persuaded by whom, men establish altars of Zeus the King, and indeed some do not shrink from addressing him as father in their prayers, as though there were some such origin and constitution of the universe. So that in this way they seem to me not even to shrink from declaring the whole universe the house of Zeus, if indeed he is father of those in it, and, by Zeus, a city too, as we likened it according to the greater principle.

37. For kingship would be more fittingly said of a city than of a house. For surely those who say that the one over the whole is king would not deny that the whole is ruled by a king, nor, having said it is ruled by a king, would they deny that it is governed as a state, nor that there is a kingly constitution of the whole. And again, granting a constitution, they would not turn aside from admitting either a city or something nearly resembling this, the thing governed.

38. This, then, is the discourse of the philosophers, declaring a good and humane fellowship of gods and men, giving a share of law and constitution not to the chance animals, but to those who have a part in reason and prudence, introducing one far better and more just than the Laconian legislation, by which it is not even possible for the Helots to become Spartans; whence indeed they continue plotting against Sparta.

39. But another story is sung, admired, in the secret rites by the men called Magi, who hymn this god as the perfect and first charioteer of the most perfect chariot. For the chariot of the Sun, they say, is newer compared with that, and visible to the many, since its course becomes evident. Whence it meets with common report, as it seems, from well-nigh the first of the poets who tell of risings and settings on each occasion, all alike expounding the horses being yoked and the Sun himself mounting the car.

40. But the strong and perfect chariot of Zeus no one of those here ever hymned worthily, neither Homer nor Hesiod, but Zoroaster and the children of the Magi sing it, having learned from him; whom the Persians say, through love of wisdom and justice, having withdrawn from the rest, lived by himself on a certain mountain; then the mountain caught fire, much fire having descended from above, and burned continually. The king, then, with the most notable of the Persians, came near, wishing to pray to the god; and the man came out of the fire unharmed, and appearing to them gracious bade them take courage and offer certain sacrifices, as the god had come to the place.

41. And afterward he consorted not with all, but with those best endowed by nature toward truth and able to understand the god, whom the Persians called Magi, knowing how to serve the divine — not as the Greeks, through ignorance of the name, so call charlatan men. And they do the rest according to sacred rules, and indeed rear for Zeus a chariot of Nisaean horses; and these are the fairest and greatest of those in Asia; but for the Sun a single horse.

42. And they expound the story not as our prophets of the Muses set forth each thing with much persuasion, but very arbitrarily. For there is, they say, one leading and charioteering of the universe, ever brought about by the highest experience and might, and this unceasing in the unceasing cycles of eternity. And the courses of the Sun and Moon, as I said, are motions of parts, whence they are seen by men more clearly. But of the motion and course of the universe the many understand not, but are ignorant of the greatness of this contest.

43. The thing after this I am ashamed to tell about the horses and the charioteering, how they say it in expounding, not greatly caring that the likeness should everywhere come out alike to them. For perhaps I should appear absurd, singing a barbarian song alongside Greek and graceful songs; yet I must venture. They say the first of the horses, on the outside, far surpasses in beauty and greatness and swiftness, since it runs round the outermost of the course, sacred to Zeus himself; and it is winged; and bright in colour, of the purest gleam; and in it the Sun and the Moon are seen as conspicuous signs, just as, I think, of these horses too there are signs, some crescent-shaped, others otherwise.

44. And these are seen by us in clusters, like strong sparks running about in the bright gleam of flame, but they have their own motion by themselves. And the other stars, appearing through that one and being all parts of it by nature, some are carried round with it, having this one motion, others run other courses. And these happen among men to have each its own name; but the rest are by multitudes in clusters, distributed into certain figures and forms.

45. The brightest, then, and most varied horse, dearest to Zeus himself, being thus somehow hymned by them, fittingly obtained first, as being first, sacrifices and honours; and the second after that, touching it and very near, named after Hera, well-reined and soft, but much inferior in might and speed. And in colour by its own nature black, but it is ever brightened, the part lit by the Sun; but the shaded part in the revolution takes again its own appearance of colour.

46. The third sacred to Poseidon, slower than the second. Of this the poets fable that an image came to be among men, it seems to me, which they call Pegasus, and they say that it loosed a spring in Corinth, cutting it with its hoof. And the fourth is, to liken it, the most absurd of all, firm and immovable, so far from being winged, named after Hestia. Yet they do not turn aside from the likeness, but say that this too has been yoked to the chariot, but remains in its place, biting an adamant bit.

47. And it presses against itself on all sides with its parts, and the two near it likewise incline toward it, simply falling upon and pushing it; but the outermost first is ever carried round the one that stands as round a turning-post. For the most part, then, they continue in peace and friendship unharmed by one another. But ere now sometimes, in length of time and many cycles, a strong gasping of the first, falling from above, as of a spirited one, heated the others, but more vehemently the last; and it scorched its mane, in which it most gloried, and the whole universe.

48. And the Greeks, remembering this experience once, they say, attribute it to Phaethon, not being able to blame the charioteering of Zeus, and not willing to censure the courses of the Sun. Therefore they say a younger charioteer, a mortal son of the Sun, having desired a grievous and disadvantageous sport for all mortals, having asked of his father to stand on the car, and being borne disorderly, scorched all animals and plants, and at last himself was destroyed, struck by a stronger fire.

49. And again, when after more years the colt sacred to the Nymphs and to Poseidon rises up, having striven and been disturbed beyond its wont, it floods with much sweat this same one, as being its yoke-fellow; it makes trial, then, of the destruction opposite to the former, storm-tossed with much water. And such one storm the Greeks relate, through their youth and weak memory, and they say Deucalion, who was then reigning over them, sufficed before the complete destruction.

50. And these things, rarely occurring, seem to men, through their own ruin, to come about not according to reason nor to share in the order of the universe, but it escapes them that they happen rightly and according to the judgment of him who saves and steers the whole. For it is like as when the charioteer of a chariot punishes one of the horses, pulling with the bit or touching with the goad; and it leaps and is disturbed, straightway being set into the needful state. This one strong charioteering, then, they speak of, the whole not being destroyed.

51. And again another of the motion and change of the four, changing into one another and exchanging their forms, until all come together into one nature, defeated by the stronger. Yet this motion too they dare to liken to charioteering and the driving of a chariot, needing a more absurd likeness; as if some juggler, having moulded horses out of wax, then, taking away and scraping from each, should add now to one, now to another, and at last, having spent all upon one of the four, should make one form out of all the material.

52. Yet such a thing is not, as in the case of soulless moulds, the craftsman working from outside and transposing the material, but the experience comes about of those very ones, as in a great and true contest striving for victory; and the victory and the crown come of necessity to the first and strongest in speed and might and the whole of virtue, whom we said at the beginning of our discourse to be the special horse of Zeus.

53. For this one, being the most valiant of all and by nature fiery, having quickly consumed the others, like, I think, in truth wax, in no long time — but seeming to us infinite by our own reckoning — and having taken into itself all the being of all, was seen far stronger and brighter than before, by no other of mortals or immortals, but itself by itself having become victorious in the greatest contest. And standing lofty and proud, rejoicing in the victory, it occupied as much room as possible and needed then a greater space through might and force.

54. Having come to this point of the discourse, they are abashed to name the same nature of the living being. For it is now at this time simply the soul of the charioteer and master, or rather the very thinking and leading part of it.

55. So indeed we too say, honouring and revering the greatest god by good deeds and well-omened words. For the mind alone being left and having filled an inconceivable place with itself, as poured out equally everywhere, nothing dense being left in it, but all rarity prevailing, when it becomes fairest, having taken the purest nature of unmixed gleam, straightway longed for the life from the beginning. Having taken love, then, of that charioteering and rule and concord of the three natures and of sun and moon and the other stars, and of all animals and plants simply, it set out to beget and distribute each thing and to fashion the universe now existing from the beginning, far stronger and brighter, as being newer.

56. And having flashed wholly, not a disorderly nor foul lightning, such as in winter often darts through the clouds when they are more violently driven, but pure and unmixed with anything dark, it changed easily along with the thought. And remembering Aphrodite and generation, it softened and relaxed itself, and having quenched much of the light, turns into a fiery air of gentle fire. And mingling then with Hera and sharing the most perfect bed, having rested it sends forth again all the seed of the universe. This the children of the wise hymn in unspeakable rites as the happy marriage of Hera and Zeus.

57. And having made the whole being moist, one seed of the universe, itself running about in this, as in the seed the breath that moulds and fashions, then indeed most resembling the constitution of the other animals, in so far as it might not absurdly be said to consist of soul and body, the rest it now easily moulds and shapes, having poured the being smooth and soft about itself and all readily yielding.

58. And having worked and perfected it, it declared from the beginning the universe now existing comely and inconceivably beautiful, far brighter than such as it is now seen. For doubtless all the other works of craftsmen too, new from the art and the hands, are at once better and more gleaming than that of the maker afterward. And of plants the newer are more flourishing than the old and wholly like shoots. And indeed the animals are graceful and pleasant to see after their birth, not only the fairest of them — colts and calves and puppies — but also the cubs of the wildest beasts.

59. For the nature of man is then infant and watery, like the imperfect green growth of Demeter, but having advanced to the measure of bloom and youth is a stronger and more conspicuous growth simply than any plant. And the whole heaven and universe, when first it was completed, adorned by the wisest and best art, just freed from the hands of the craftsman, bright and translucent and shining in all its parts, was an infant for no time nor weak according to the human and mortal weakness of nature, but young and at its prime straightway from the beginning.

60. When indeed its craftsman and father, seeing it, was in no way pleased — for this is a low experience among the low — but rejoiced and was delighted exceedingly, seated on Olympus, and his heart laughed for gladness, when he saw the gods all now come into being and present. And the form of the universe then — I mean the bloom and the beauty, it being ever inconceivably beautiful — no man could conceive and tell worthily, neither of those now nor of those before, save the Muses and Apollo in divine rhythm of pure and supreme harmony.

61. Whence indeed let us too now leave off, not having shrunk from raising the discourse so far as was possible for us. But if the form of the discourse turned out simply lofty and faint — as those clever about the birds say that the one that has gone very high up and hidden itself in the clouds makes the divination imperfect — it is not right to blame me, but the request of the Borysthenites, since they then bade me speak thus.

1. When I first sojourned in your city, about ten years ago, and gave the people and your magistrates a share of my discourses, I seemed to be acceptable, and that too to you so very much as not even Arion the Methymnaean. Of Arion, at least, you did not make a likeness. And when I say "you," I mean your ancestors and Periander the son of Cypselus, the wise, in whose time Arion lived, who also first of men composed the dithyramb and named it and taught it in Corinth.

2. For he was so beloved of the gods that, sailing up hither with great wealth which he had earned about Tarentum and the Greeks there, when he was about to be thrown into the sea by the sailors on account, doubtless, of this very wealth, he begged them before the throwing to let him sing — just as they say the swans, when about to die and foreseeing death, embark their soul as it were upon the song as upon a chariot.

3. So then he sang — for there was a calm and stillness over the sea — and the dolphins perceived the song, and perceiving it were about the ship. And when Arion had ceased and the sailors yielded nothing soft, he flung himself into the deep, and a dolphin coming under bore the singer to Taenarum as he was, with his equipment. Arion, then, having been thus saved and having forestalled the sailors, was in Corinth, relating these very things to Periander.

4. And when the sailors put in and the matter was brought to proof, they were put to death; but Arion — for it was not Periander, but Arion — having made a bronze likeness, not large, dedicated it at Taenarum, himself seated upon his benefactor.
