And about this same time both Solon was in Corinth, fleeing the tyranny of Peisistratus, but not fleeing that of Periander.

5. For it was not the same: the one, having abolished the democracy, was tyrant of the Athenians, but Periander had received the kingship from his father, whom the Greeks called tyrant, but the gods king. Or does not the oracle run thus? Blessed is this man who comes to my house, Cypselus son of Eetion, king of glorious Corinth, himself and his children.

6. Of whom one was Periander himself, who succeeded his father. So then Periander was by the god proclaimed king, but by the Greeks wise; than whom no king or tyrant ever acquired a greater name; not even Antiochus surnamed the god, nor Mithridates the Dionysus. And Pittacus the Mytilenaean would have prayed to be called both at once, both tyrant and wise; but as it is, clinging to the second name, he put off the tyranny. Periander was wise with the few, but tyrant with the many;

7. but both, tyrant and wise, he alone. To him Solon came and shared in the common things — for friends' things are common — but nonetheless did not obtain a statue, not, doubtless, despising a statue, but making much even of standing in bronze in Salamis; how then not in Corinth, in the promenade of Greece? And Herodotus the chronicler came too to you, bringing Greek tales, both others and ones about the Corinthians not yet false, in return for which he thought fit to win a reward from the city. But failing of this too — for your ancestors did not think fit to buy reputation — he recast those things which we all know, the matters about Salamis and Adeimantus.

8. But us, when we sojourned twice, you so gladly beheld that you most of all tried to keep us, and seeing it was impossible, at least you made the likeness of our body and bearing it dedicated it in the library, in the front place, where you would most think to incite the young to cling to the same pursuits as ours. For not as one of the many who put in yearly at Cenchreae, a merchant or pilgrim or envoy or one passing through, but as one scarcely after long intervals appearing and welcome, so you honoured us.

9. But honour, like a dream taking wing, has flown away. So that I am at a loss both with myself and, by Zeus, now with another, whether truly I did not see nor was awake, but what was happening was a dream, or whether these things were so in all exactness — the eagerness of the people and the decision of the council — but the statue happened to be one of the works of Daedalus and, escaping our notice, ran away.

10. But since Daedalus died, no one to this day has attained to such art as even to put flight into the bronze; rather they make them striding well and beautifully, and some borne even upon horses; yet all these remain in figure and place, even if no one moves them, so far as in them lies the bronze that cannot run, even if it have wings, like the Perseus of Pythagoras.

11. But that it might even be of the ancient Daedalian art, what suffering would have made it depart from your city, about which they say the two gods strove, Poseidon and the Sun, the one master of fire, the other of water? And having striven and entrusted the arbitration to a third god, an elder, of whom are most heads and most hands, having entrusted the arbitration to this one, both hold this city and the country — no small nor obscure sign of its superiority over the rest.

12. For the other allotments and possessions of the gods are single: Argos is Hera's, and Athens Athena's; and of these very gods, Rhodes is the Sun's, Onchestus Poseidon's, but Corinth both. You might conjecture that the myth hints at this — that the spot, in the midst of two seas, was made special by the Sun with Poseidon's consent. Now the matter of the myth and the discourse,

13. somewhat consonant with this, calls upon a third, beyond the two witnesses, the prophetic Sibyl; and she, having received a clear voice from the god, sings very loudly: Happy is the pine-clad blessed neck of Ephyra, daughter of Ocean, where Poseidon, father of my mother Lamia, first set up a contest together with the Sun, and bore away the honours alone.

14. And indeed they say the first contest was set up here by the two gods, and that Castor won the stadium-race, and Calais the double course — for they say Calais ran, abstaining from flying. And the rest too, since we have begun, must be named prize-winners and victors. Orpheus in the lyre, Heracles in the all-in fight, Polydeuces in boxing, Peleus in wrestling, Telamon in the discus, Theseus in the armed contest. And a horse-race too was set up, and Phaethon won with the single horse, Neleus with the four-horse chariot.

15. And there was a contest of ships too, and the Argo won, and after that she did not sail, but Jason dedicated her here to Poseidon, and inscribed the epigram which they say is Orpheus': I am the hull Argo, and Jason dedicated me to the god, crowned with the pine of the Isthmus and of Nemea. But where gods preside over the games, and demigods conquer and are conquered, and the Argo rests, what fairer place than this could Daedalus himself have found, flying with wings — to say nothing of the work of Daedalus?

16. But it neither ran away nor attempted it nor at all intended it. It remains, then, that the Corinthians themselves cast it out, neither with a trial set nor having at all any charge to bring. And was anyone persuaded of this against the Corinthians, whose ancestors of all the Greeks most practised justice? For are not these the men who abolish the tyrannies in the cities and establish the democracies and freed Athens from the tyrants,

17. formerly from Hippias, later from Cleomenes, and after this, when the Athenians themselves attempted to do the work of Hippias and Isagoras and to establish a tyranny over Greece, were the first to perceive it and most grieved by it, and became leaders of freedom to the rest, and preserved this purpose not only in the case of the Athenians, but also in the case of the Lacedaemonians? For they opposed the Lacedaemonians too, on behalf of the common rights of Greece, with the city of the Thebans and the Eleans; by which they also showed that they were not pro-Laconian, but simply lovers of Greece and of justice and of freedom and haters of wickedness and of tyrants.

18. For they were such haters of the barbarian that to Thermopylae they sent four hundred of themselves, when the Lacedaemonians too sent three hundred. And at Salamis they were the bravest and became the cause of the victory. For I do not heed Herodotus, but the tomb and Simonides, who inscribed upon the dead of the Corinthians buried in Salamis: O stranger, once we dwelt in the well-watered city of Corinth, but now the isle of Ajax, Salamis, holds us. And easily, having taken the Phoenician ships and the Persians and Medes, we established sacred Greece.

19. And there is another epigram of Simonides upon the general himself, a special one: This is the tomb of that Adeimantus, through whose counsels Greece put on the crown of freedom. And they freed Sicily too from the barbarians, and Syracuse from the tyrants. And one might see Dionysius in Corinth, a most beautiful spectacle, master of nothing; but nonetheless no one wronged him either, nor cast him out nor drove him of those from Sicily.

20. But the dedication of the city, who overturned it? Surely not a whirlwind or hurricane or thunderbolt falling, shaking and directing the lightning. But if there is some judging of a statue, such as they say happened in Syracuse — and the manner I shall not shrink from telling, throwing it in: the Syracusans, your colonists, in many wars against the Carthaginians and the other barbarians who inhabit Sicily and Italy, had run short of bronze and of coinage;

21. they voted, then, to break up the statues of the tyrants — and many of these were among them made of bronze — having made a judgment among them, who of them was worthy to be melted down and who not; and he prevails in the trial — that you may hear this too — Gelon the son of Deinomenes; and all the rest were broken up, except indeed Dionysius the elder of those clad in the form of Dionysus —

22. but if there should be among you too some such decree, that there be a reckoning of statues — or rather, if you will, as though this had been voted and a contest were at hand, grant me, grant me to make the speech on its behalf before you as in a court. Men, judges, all things, they say, one must expect in the long time; but this one in the short time runs the risk of having been set up as the best of the Greeks, but of being cast out as the most wicked.

23. That, then, it was set up nobly and justly and advantageously for your city and for all the Greeks, though I have much to say, I wish to relate to you one thing that happened in that very Syracuse. For the example is appropriate; and it is just, perhaps, that as they honour the mother-city, so you too should imitate the deeds of your colony, whichever are noble.

24. They, then, in those ancient times, a certain Lucanian man, because he reported some embassy to the people in Doric, being pleased with his speech, both sent him away not unsuccessful in the matters for which he had come, and presented him with a talent, and set up the likeness of his body — from the neighbouring states and the Dorians there, both the others and those inhabiting Italy — as having repaid the man well and nobly on behalf of the Doric race, whose speech he had practised to the point of being able to speak it.

25. But if one not being a Lucanian, but a Roman, nor of the common people, but of the equestrian order, has emulated not the speech only, but also the judgment and the way of life and the bearing of the Greeks, and that too so resolutely and conspicuously as none of the Romans before him nor of the Greeks of his own time — for it shall be said — not one; for of the Greeks one may see the best inclining there toward the affairs of the Romans, but the foremost man inclining toward the affairs of the Greeks, and for these things giving up his substance and his political rank and everything simply, that he may have left him one thing in place of all — to seem and to be a Greek — then ought not such a man to stand in bronze among you?

26. And city by city: among you, because, being a Roman, he was Hellenized, as your fatherland was; among the Athenians, because he speaks Attic; among the Lacedaemonians, because he loves gymnastics; among all, because he loves wisdom and has already roused many of the Greeks to philosophize with him, and has drawn not a few of the barbarians too.

27. For to this very end he seemed to have been fashioned by the gods, as it were on purpose: for the Greeks, that the natives of Greece might have an example that being educated differs nothing from being born so toward seeming; for the Romans, that not even those clad in their own peculiar dignity should overlook education for the sake of dignity; for the Celts, that none even of the barbarians should despair of Greek education, looking to this man. He was set up, then, for such reasons (that I may not, saying more, seem to lead myself into hatred),

28. but it is not the same thing to deliberate about the setting up of a likeness and about its taking down. Why? Because each of these dedicated among you, whether better or worse, is now clad with sanctity, and the city ought to preside over it as over a dedication. One might have much to say that Gorgias the sophist ought not to stand in Delphi, and that too aloft and golden. Gorgias, do I say? When one may see even Phryne the Thespian, she too upon a column, like Gorgias.

29. But to oppose at once is perhaps lawful and political; but, having come afterward to the dedication, to try to dissolve what has been resolved — Apollo, that is grievous; and none of the Amphictyons would have endured it. For even if they were set up when they ought not, having forestalled by the setting up, they stand as they ought, from the time they forestalled it. For just as of those chosen for a year, even if one be unworthy of office, yet for that year at least into which he was chosen archon he continues, so for the statues too the time must be valid for which they were set up; and this is all the remaining time.

30. Or in what will you differ from those who mould figures of clay? And what fine thing will you have to say to those who demand of you a reason why with you the honours are mortal, but the dishonours immortal? If, then, this is in no way shameful, though it is dreadful, are not yearly statues, like the crops, the mark of an altogether conceited polity? For those whom you set up in bronze not that they may straightway perish, but that they may abide the longest time, these you declare softer even than the waxen ones.

31. Or, by Zeus, because it befell that they were seen to be wicked afterward? If they became so afterward, this does not release the city from blame; for you give the honours not for the future, but for the past. But if, being such before, he was descried afterward, in which of the two ways do you think one would be the more of good repute among the Greeks, and in which would you the more incite those who wish to do you good — by making the decision liable to retrial, or by abiding in what was once resolved? I, for my part, think thus. For the one is the mark of unfortunate men, the other of steadfast ones.

32. I do not yet say the greatest thing, that it must be not from slander, but from condemnation, nor from any chance charge, but from the greatest, that so great an honour, if indeed it must, be overturned. For as concerns slander, even Socrates would be a corruptor of the young and an overthrower of all things believed among men, beginning from the gods. For whom have these men not slandered, who slander everything? Not Socrates? Not Pythagoras? Not Plato? Not Zeus himself and Poseidon and Apollo and the other gods?

33. And they lay hands on the female deities too, of whom it were fitting to be more in awe than of the male. For now you hear what they say of Demeter and Aphrodite and Eos; and they abstain not even from Athena nor from Artemis; but the one they strip bare for Actaeon, the other they even unite to Hephaestus and make the virgin all but a mother. Knowing these things, then, do you marvel if against this man too some censure has been spread abroad, which it has been possible for no one of all who have lived in repute to escape, but which took its occasion from his — whether one must call it charm in his discourses or whatever — this which you too with wives and children approved?

34. Will you not consider? Will you not call to mind among yourselves, whether any such thing has been done by him among you? And yet you inhabit a city the most charming of those that are and have been, but nonetheless you heard nothing, and I would say with confidence that no other of the Greeks did either. Then do you think that the man who lived decorously in Greece, with more impunity and indulgence, has in Rome, beside the very ruler and the laws, changed? But this is much as if one should say that the athlete is well-behaved by himself, but in the stadium and before the games-president plays false.

35. And I have a double frankness, one on account of the conscience, the other of the games-president. For it belonged to one who believed to take vengeance on the offender, but to one who had heard to be wroth; which that man did. But you followed certain men — but I will say nothing against them as in revenge; except that it were more just for them to follow you than you them.

36. For you are now, as the saying is, the prow and the stern of Greece, called blessed and wealthy and the like names from ancient times by the poets and the gods, when it belonged to some others too both to be rich and to be powerful; but now, since wealth has forsaken Orchomenus and Delphi, they can surpass you in pity, but not one in envy.

37. And these things are on behalf of the city, which ought not to incur shame among the Greeks, when him whom you have cast out all gladly receive — not only, but also invite and send embassies and honour with the other honours and indeed with the dedication of likenesses. But on behalf of myself and the likeness I will now say a word which Anaxagoras spoke, having lost a son: I knew I had begotten a mortal. But I knew that each of these statues is dedicated as though it will be eternal, but perishes one by one fate, another by another — the most common and most just and set before all things, that of time;

38. but the poet who made this epigram boasted vainly, which they say was written upon the tomb of Midas: I am a bronze maiden, and I lie upon the tomb of Midas. So long as water flows and tall trees flourish, remaining here on the much-wept tomb, I shall announce to those passing by that Midas is buried here.

39. But, O self-announcing maiden, we hear the poet, but seeking you we found you not, nor the tomb of Midas. And those waters and trees still flow and flourish, but in time these too, with the rest, seem likely to fail, like Midas, like the maiden. A man's name was Hippaemon, the horse's Podargus, and the dog's Lethargus, and the servant's Babes. Who, then, of the Greeks knows not — I do not say the horse, but Hippaemon himself? Not even of the Magnesians, I think, whence Hippaemon was. He, then, is gone from among men, he and Babes and Podargus.

40. But others stand and are recognized, but have the inscription of others, and the thing that happens is like the antispast in lyrics: the inscription speaks Roman, and in a manner the poets teach the contrary; for they have the manner of the Greeks, but the fortunes of the Romans. I beheld also the fair Alcibiades, the son of Cleinias — I know not where, except I beheld in a fine part of Greece — having the inscription of Chalcopogon, and another with his hands cut off, which was said to be of the art of Polycles; a dreadful sight, O Earth and Sun, Alcibiades maimed.

41. And I know that Harmodius and Aristogeiton served as slaves among the Persians, and that the fifteen hundred statues of Demetrius of Phalerum were all taken down by the Athenians in one and the same day. And they dared even to pour chamber-pots over Philip the king. The Athenians, then, poured urine over the likeness, but that man poured over the city blood and ashes and dust. For it was indeed a thing to provoke nemesis, the same man being now spoken of among the gods, now not even among men.

42. Then I, knowing these things, that men do not spare even the gods, do you think I take thought for a statue? And the rest I think I shall pass over in silence; but the Isthmian, your games-president, Mummius, having torn him up from his base, dedicated to Zeus — alas for the ignorance — his brother as a dedication, an uneducated man and one who had had trial of none of the noble things. Who inscribed Philip the son of Amyntas, whom he took from Thespiae, as Zeus, and the young men from Pheneus the one as Nestor, the other as Priam. And the people of the Romans thought to see in this that famous thing, the descendants of that man, seeing Arcadians from Pheneus.

43. These things, then, one may even laugh at. But in earnest it has come to me to call Agesilaus the king of the Lacedaemonians blessed for his judgment, who never thought fit either to have a moulded or imitated likeness of his body made — not because he was lame, as they say, and small (for what hindered the statue from being great? what from being sound of foot, like the Hephaestus of Euphranor?) — but he saw this exactly, that one must not stretch out human fortunes nor risk anything about the body in stone and bronze. Would that one could be rid even of the body.

44. But farewell to Daedalus and the imitative artworks of Daedalus; enough of Prometheus, enough of clay. And yet they say even the body of the noble is alien, since there are very many things between body and soul. For the one is not, nor cares for the body when it suffers. Cambyses was mad, in that he pricked and scourged the corpse of Amasis the king of the Egyptians. For the Egyptians say that Amasis, long suspecting the harshness of Cambyses, hid his own corpse and substituted another in its stead, and that this was the one that fell into Cambyses' hands.

45. But, O Egyptians and Cambyses, whether it was someone else who suffered these things or Amasis himself, it was a figure bloodless, fleshless, soulless. This, if you please, drag and tear and prick, but Amasis you have not laid hold of. But another, living, breathing, perceiving, said: Pound, pound the sack of Anaxarchus; for Anaxarchus you do not pound. For this man, having fallen into a mortar and being struck with the pestles, himself said he was not being pounded, but that of his own which happened to be wrapped about him; just as they say the peers among the Persians take their blows on the kandys instead of the body.

46. The Persians, then, are vexed at this; but a Greek man offered his body to be beaten as a kandys, as a cloak; and shall we not offer the statue to be melted down, even if it perceive? But now the one is beyond perception, while I, like the Laodameia of Euripides, would not betray a friend even though soulless. I wish, then, to console it as though perceiving. O silent image of my words, do you not appear? For neither did Aristeas before you; for thus it was with him too, as I conjecture: that he was set up by the Proconnesians, but made to vanish by his enemies; and that a report was spread by these same men, that Aristeas appeared neither living nor dead. But both then and now and for all time Aristeas lived.

47. I say that another too shall remember us. For Sappho said it very well; and much more nobly Hesiod: Report no one wholly perishes, whatsoever many peoples voice abroad; she too is some goddess. I will set you up beside the goddess, whence none shall take you down — not earthquake, not wind, not snow, not rain, not envy, not enemy; but even now I find you standing. For oblivion has ere now tripped up and deceived some others too, but the judgment of good men has deceived no one, by which you stand upright before me, man by man.

1. Democritus speaks thus of Homer: "Homer, having been allotted a divinely-inspired nature, fashioned an array of verses of every kind" — as though it were not possible, without a divine and superhuman nature, to work out verses so fine and wise. And many others too have written, some praising the poet outright while at the same time expounding some of the things said by him, others setting forth this very thing, his meaning — not only Aristarchus and Crates and several others of those afterward called grammarians, but formerly critics. And indeed Aristotle himself, from whom they say criticism and grammar took their origin, goes through the poet in many dialogues, admiring him for the most part and honouring him; and besides, Heraclides of Pontus.
2. And earlier than these, Plato everywhere makes mention of him — struck with astonishment at the pleasure and grace of the verses, yet often blaming him in the matter of the tales and accounts about the gods, on the ground that he has spoken what is in no way profitable to men, going through their graspings and plots against one another, and adulteries, and quarrels, and contentions among the gods; and thereafter not giving him a share in his own city and polity, which was to be wise, as he thought — in order that the young, whom he sets up as guardians and leaders of the city, may neither hear these things about the gods, nor again, by anything gloomy being said about the things in Hades, be made softer toward fighting and toward dying, nor, like colts badly broken in from the start, be made shy at things not fearful.
3. About these things, indeed, there is another argument, fuller and longer and not easy: whether Homer erred in these matters, or whether he was handing on to men, according to the custom of that time, certain physical doctrines contained in the tales. For it is not easy to arbitrate such a thing — just as, I think, when two men who are friends, both august, the one charging the other,
4. to give judgement against one of them. And Zeno the philosopher too wrote upon both the Iliad and the Odyssey, and about the Margites as well; for this poem too seems to have been composed by Homer when he was younger and was making trial of his own nature for poetry. And Zeno blames nothing of Homer's, while at the same time expounding and teaching that he wrote some things according to opinion, others according to truth, so that he may not appear to be at odds with himself in certain things that seem to be said in a contrary sense.
5. But this argument is Antisthenes' earlier — that some things are spoken by the poet according to opinion, others according to truth; only the one did not work it out, while the other made it plain in each of the particulars. And besides, Persaeus the disciple of Zeno wrote according to the same thesis, and several others. And Plato, while at once accusing him, as I said, declares the power of his poetry to be something marvellous, since it is an image of every thing and simply gives forth all voices — of rivers and winds and waves; and he bids them, very ironically, crown him with wool and pour myrrh over him and send him away to others.
6. This the women do in the case of swallows. And besides, he himself, going over the grace of the poetry, exceedingly admires the man. For simply, not without divine fortune, nor without the inspiration of the Muses and of Apollo, was it possible for poetry so lofty and magnificent, and moreover so pleasant, to come into being — so as to hold sway, for so long a time now, not only over those of the same tongue and speech, but over many of the barbarians too; and that those of double tongue and of mixed race are exceedingly familiar with his verses, though ignorant of much else that is Greek, and some even of those settled very far away — since they say that among the Indians too the poetry of Homer is sung, they having translated it into their own dialect and speech.
7. So that, though the Indians are without sight of many of the stars among us — for they say the Bears do not appear with them — they are not unacquainted with the sufferings of Priam, and the laments and wailings of Andromache and Hecuba, and the valour of Achilles and Hector. So great power had the music of one man; and he seems to me by this power to have surpassed both the Sirens and Orpheus.
8. For to charm and lead stones and plants and beasts — what else is it than so utterly to master barbarian men who do not understand the Greek tongue, men experienced neither in the language nor in the matters of which the discourse treats, but simply charmed, as I think, as if by the lyre? And I, for my part, think that many even of the more ignorant barbarians have heard at least the name of Homer, but do not clearly know what it signifies, whether a living creature or a plant or some other thing.
9. Nonetheless, one might praise the man's life far more than his poetry. For to have lived in poverty and as a wanderer, providing from his poems just enough to live by, is a sign of marvellous courage and magnanimity; and besides, that he nowhere wrote his own name, nor even made mention of himself in his poetry — and that too while all the rest, as many as seemed to have any power, whether in poetry or in writing prose, wrote their own name both first and last, and many even within the discourses and poems themselves,
10. as did Hecataeus and Herodotus and Thucydides — and he, indeed, not once only at the beginning of the history, but often, declaring solemnly at each winter and summer that "Thucydides composed these things" — but he was so free and magnanimous that he will nowhere be found making mention of his own poetry, but in truth, like the prophets of the gods, uttering his words from somewhere unseen and inaccessible.
11. And that everything he wrote is profitable and useful — to go through the rest, all that he composed about virtue and vice, would be much labour; but about kings, in brief, what manner of men he says they ought to be. For whomever of the kings he praises, he says is "in counsel a match for Zeus," and all the good kings "nurtured of Zeus"; and Minos, who has the greatest reputation for justice among the Greeks, he says was the companion and disciple of Zeus — as though that one were the first and greatest king of all, and alone knew and handed on the kingly art, and as though the good kings ought, looking to him, to direct their rule aright, making their own manner like, so far as is possible for men, to god.
12. And the character of Zeus, and what his kingship was like, he makes plain in many other places; but, to embrace his power and his thought in brief, he often shows it, ever naming him thus, "father of men and of gods" — as though the care of kings ought to be fatherly and protecting, with goodwill and friendship, and as though it never befits one to preside over and rule men otherwise than by cherishing them and taking forethought for them, since Zeus does not disdain to be called father of men.

1. Since you appear to be in other respects an admirer of Socrates and to be struck with wonder at the man in your discourses, can you tell me whose disciple among the wise he was — as Pheidias the maker of statues was of Hegias, and Polygnotus the painter and his brother both of their father Aglaophon, and Pherecydes is said to have become the teacher of Pythagoras, and Pythagoras of Empedocles and others, and of most of the rest we can tell the teachers of the famous men, by associating with whom each became worthy of mention — save only Heraclitus of Ephesus and Hesiod of Ascra? For the one says that, tending his flocks on Helicon, he received his poetry from the Muses in a sprig of laurel, that we may have no trouble seeking his teacher;
2. and Heraclitus, still more nobly, that he himself discovered the nature of the universe, of what sort it is, with no one teaching him, and became wise from himself. For of Homer, as the other things about him, so this too is unclear to the Greeks. But of Socrates we have heard that, when a boy, he learned his father's craft as a stone-cutter; but the teacher of his wisdom, which proved so profitable and fine — do you tell us clearly, and do not grudge it.
3. D. Why, this at least, I think, is clear to many — to whoever is acquainted with both men — that Socrates in truth became a disciple of Homer, not, as some say, of Archelaus. — And how is it possible to call him a disciple of Homer who neither associated with Homer nor ever saw him, but was born so many years after Homer? — D. What then? Whoever was born in Homer's time, but heard none of Homer's verses, or, hearing, gave heed to none of them — is there any way we shall call that man a disciple of Homer? —
4. By no means. — D. Is it not strange, then, that the man who neither associated with him nor saw him, but understood the poetry of Homer and became acquainted with his whole thought, should be called a disciple of Homer? Or will you say that no one is an emulator of anyone among those who did not associate with him? — I, for one, will. — D. If, then, he is an emulator, he would also be a disciple. For he who rightly emulates someone surely knows that man, of what sort he was, and, imitating his deeds and words so far as he can, endeavours to make himself like him.
5. And this same thing the disciple too seems to do: imitating his teacher and giving heed, he takes up the art. But seeing and associating is nothing toward learning; for many both see the flute-players and associate with them and hear them daily, and yet could not even blow upon the flutes — those, that is, who associate with them not with a view to the art, nor giving heed. But if you scruple to call Socrates a disciple of Homer, and call him only an emulator, it will make no difference to me. —
6. To me this seems no less strange than the other. For Homer was a poet such as no other; but Socrates a philosopher. — D. So be it; on that reckoning you would not call even Archilochus an emulator of Homer, because he did not use the same metre for his whole poetry, but other metres for the most part; nor Stesichorus, because the one composed epic verses, while Stesichorus was a lyric poet. —
7. Yes; this at least all the Greeks say — that Stesichorus became an emulator of Homer and very greatly resembled him in his poetry. But in what respect does Socrates seem to you to resemble Homer? — D. First and chiefly in character. For neither of them was a boaster nor shameless, like the most ignorant of the sophists. For Homer did not even think fit to say whence he was, nor of what parents, nor by what name he himself was called; but, for all of him, we should not even have known the name of the man who wrote the Iliad and the Odyssey.
8. Socrates, on the other hand, could not conceal his fatherland, because of the greatness and the very great renown of Athens, and because she ruled the Greeks at that time; yet he never said anything great about himself, nor laid claim to any wisdom, though Apollo had given the oracle that he was wisest of Greeks and barbarians. And at the last he himself did not leave his discourses behind in writing — and in this at least he surpassed Homer. For just as we know the name of that man by hearing it from others, so too we know the discourses of Socrates because others left them behind. So exceedingly chastened and prudent were both the men.
9. Then they alike disdained the acquisition of money, both Socrates and Homer. And besides, they were both in earnest about the same things and discoursed of them — the one through poetry, the other in prose: about the virtue and vice of men, and about errors and right actions, and about truth and deception, and how the many opine and how the prudent know. And indeed they were both most apt at likening and comparing. — This is wonderful, if to the comparisons of Homer — of fire and winds and the sea and eagles and bulls and lions and the rest, with which Homer adorned his poetry — you will think fit to compare the potters and the cobblers of Socrates. —
10. D. Yes, my good friend — if indeed we also compare the fox of Archilochus to lions and leopards and say it falls short in nothing, or not by much. But perhaps you reject such things even in Homer — where he makes mention of starlings or jackdaws or locusts or a firebrand or ashes or beans and chickpeas, or has portrayed men winnowing — but these you think the meanest things of Homer's;
11. and you admire only the lions and the eagles and the Scyllas and the Cyclopes, with which he charmed the insensible, as nurses do children by telling them of the Lamia. And indeed, just as Homer endeavoured through myths and stories to educate men — who are very hard to educate — so too Socrates often used such a method, now confessing to be in earnest, now pretending to jest; and for this reason he benefited men, though perhaps he gave offence to the mythologists and the prose-writers.
12. Nor, then, did he make Gorgias or Polus or Thrasymachus or Prodicus or Meno or Euthyphro or Anytus or Alcibiades or Laches speak in vain, when he might have removed the names; but he knew that by this above all he would benefit his hearers, if somehow they should understand. For to discern men from their words, and words from the men, is not easy for any but philosophers and the educated. The many, however, suppose that such things are said in vain, and reckon them a mere crowd of names and idle babble.
13. But Socrates held that, as often as he brings in a boastful man, he is speaking about boastfulness; and whenever a shameless and loathsome one, about shamelessness and loathsomeness; and whenever an unfeeling and irascible one, that he is turning men away from unfeelingness and anger. And in the case of the rest likewise, he showed the passions and the diseases more clearly upon the very men possessed by the passions or the diseases than if he had spoken his discourses bare.
14. And this too seems to me he took from Homer. For that poet, whenever he relates of Dolon — how he desired the horses of Achilles, and how, able to escape the enemy, he stood still when the spear was fixed near him and his swiftness profited him nothing, and how he chattered with fear and clashed his teeth together, and how he told the enemy not only whatever they asked, but also things about which no one inquired (for he disclosed the Thracian horses and Rhesus, whose arrival no one knew of) — relating these things so very vividly, does he not seem to you to be discoursing of cowardice and love of glory?
15. And whenever he tells of Pandarus — how he broke the truce, hoping for gifts from Alexander son of Priam, and neither slew Menelaus by his shot, though reputed a competent archer, and, transgressing the oaths, made the Trojans more dispirited toward the war, ever mindful of the perjury: "But now, having sworn false to faithful oaths, we fight; wherefore nothing is the better for us";
16. and the manner in which he died, his tongue cut out not long after, before Alexander could so much as say in words that he was grateful to him — relating these things so carefully, does he seem to be speaking about anything other than bribe-taking and impiety and, in sum, folly? — Pandarus, who even cursed his arrows and threatened to break them in pieces and burn them, as though the arrows feared him.
17. And whenever he tells of Asius son of Hyrtacus — that, when the general had ordered them to leave the horses outside the trench, he alone did not obey, but "drove up with them close to the swift ships, the fool; nor was he, escaping the evil fates, destined, exulting in horses and chariot, to return back again from the ships to windy Ilium" —
18. driving into such difficult ground of trench and wall and ships, where it did not even profit the foot-soldiers, who were caught by the enemy, but, a small sally being made, the greater part perished; while he, lifted up by his horses and the beauty of his chariot, thought to drive over the wall, and was ready, having plunged into the sea, to fight from his car — does he not then appear to be speaking about disobedience and boastfulness?
19. And again, setting beside these Polydamas, bidding them be wary and not cross the trench, both showing the matter to be perilous and at the same time the omen that had come to them — for otherwise he thought no one would endure his speaking, but with the omen he might perhaps persuade Hector; or Nestor, stopping from their anger those who were reviling about Agamemnon and Achilles, and plainly foretelling what would befall them from the faction, and afterward rebuking Agamemnon as one who had erred and compelling him to entreat Achilles; or Odysseus correcting the error of Agamemnon, who, wishing through it to test the army, how they would bear the protraction of the war, came near to making them flee — does he not seem to be teaching about prudence and generalship and divination, and besides these, about timeliness and untimeliness?
20. And in the Odyssey I let the rest be, and will mention one only, Antinous. For him he has made the most boastful of the suitors and the most licentious; who, first, despised Odysseus because he was in rags, while he himself was in costly raiment, and drank from golden cups — and those not his own — and dined sumptuously, not from his own patrimony, but sponging upon a masterless house; and he said he was in love with Penelope, yet consorted with the maidservants of Odysseus and in other respects was licentious — not as some men now;
21. and at the last he tried to shoot, being inexperienced in archery and his hands so ruined by luxury that he could not even touch the bowstring unless someone should smear it with fat — and that too with Odysseus looking on and his beloved present, among so many men — being unable even to bend the bow, nor understanding how Telemachus would set up the axes. Nonetheless, the poet made this man too, when he died, struck not at random through the throat, not just anywhere — just as, indeed, Pandarus through the tongue. For even if such things befall by some chance, yet in many cases one may say that this man ought to die struck through the belly, that one through the private parts, that one through the mouth.
22. Does Homer, then, seem to you to say anything at random? Nor, then, did Socrates use his discourses or his examples idly, but in conversing with Anytus he made mention of tanners and cobblers; and if he conversed with Lysicles, of lambs and fleeces; with Lycon, of lawsuits and false accusations; with Meno the Thessalian, of lovers and beloveds. Yet he was also at no loss for other examples on occasion, naming friends and friendship when he conversed with Lysis, and about temperance when conversing with Charmides.

1. Men desire above all things to be free, and they say that freedom is the greatest of goods, but that slavery is the most shameful and most wretched thing of all; yet this very thing—what it is to be free or what it is to be a slave—they do not know. And so, accordingly, they do nothing, one may say, to escape the shameful and grievous thing, slavery, and to acquire what seems to them worth much, freedom; but, on the contrary, they do the very things from which it must follow that those who practise them continue slaves the whole time and never attain to freedom.

2. Yet these men perhaps it is not worth wondering at, that they can neither win nor guard against a thing of which they happen to be ignorant. For if they happened to be ignorant of a sheep and a wolf, what each of the two is, yet held the one to be useful and a good thing to acquire, the other harmful and disadvantageous, it would be nothing wonderful if they feared the sheep and sometimes fled from it as a wolf, but admitted the wolf and abode with it, supposing it a sheep; for ignorance works such things upon those who do not know, and compels them to flee and pursue the opposite of what they wish and of what is beneficial.

3. Come, then, let us consider whether the many really know anything clear about freedom and slavery. For perhaps we accuse them in vain, and they, more than anything, know these things. If, then, one should ask them what it is to be free, they would say, perhaps, that it is to be subject to no one, but simply to do whatever seems good to oneself.

4. But the man who has answered thus, if one should ask him further whether a chorus-singer in a chorus, who pays no heed to the leader nor is subject to him, but sings and sings out of tune as it occurs to him—whether he thinks this fine and freeman-like, and the opposite of it, to attend to and obey the leader of the chorus, and to begin and to cease singing whenever that man bids, shameful and slavish—I do not think he would agree.

5. Nor, if one should ask whether a man at sea who pays no heed to the steersman and does not do whatever that man tells him—whether he should think such a thing freeman-like: for instance, when bidden to sit he stands in the ship, if it does not occur to him to obey, and when bidden at some time to bail or to haul in the sails, neither bails nor lays hand to the ropes—would he call this man free or enviable, because he does what seems good to himself.

6. And certainly he would not say that soldiers are slaves, because they are subject to the general, and rise up whenever he commands, and take their rations and take up their arms and form ranks and advance and retreat in no other way than as the general orders; nor again the sick, because they obey the physicians—not for this will they say that they are slaves;

7. and yet it is in no small nor easy matters that they obey them, but they are sometimes ordered even to hunger and thirst; and if it ever seems good to the physician to bind the patient, he is bound on the spot, and if to cut or to cauterize, he will be cauterized and cut so far as it seems good to that man; and if he does not obey, all in the household will join the physician in the struggle—not only the free men, but often the very slaves of the sick man bind down their master, and bring the fire that he may be cauterized, and render the rest of the service.

8. Will you not, then, say that this man is free, because he submits to many disagreeable things at another's bidding? For surely you would not say that Darius, the king of the Persians, was not free, because, having fallen from his horse in the hunt, his ankle having gone out of joint, he obeyed the physicians who pulled and twisted his foot, that the joint might be set—and these too Egyptian men; nor again Xerxes, when, retiring from Greece and tossed by storm in the ship, he obeyed the steersman in everything, and contrary to that man's judgment did not permit himself even to nod or to shift his place. Then they will no longer say that to be subject to no man, nor to do whatever one wishes, is freedom.

9. But perhaps they will say that these men obey for their own advantage, as those at sea obey the steersman and the soldiers the general, and the sick obey the physician for this reason. For these prescribe nothing else than what is advantageous to them. But masters do not command slaves the things that will profit them, but what they think profits themselves.

10. What then? Is it advantageous to the master that the slave should die, or be sick, or be wicked? No one would say so, but, on the contrary, I think, that he should live and be healthy and be good. And these same things will appear advantageous to the slave too; so that the master, no less—if indeed he has sense—will prescribe to the slave the things advantageous to him; for these appear advantageous to himself also.

11. But whoever it is for whom a man has paid down silver, this man is of necessity a slave. Have not many men, then, paid down silver for many free men—some giving ransom to enemies, some to brigands, and some have paid down their own ransom-price to their masters? And surely these are not therefore the slaves of those men.

12. But surely the man whom another is permitted to scourge and bind and put to death and do whatever else he wishes—this man is that other's slave. What then? Are not brigands permitted to do these things to those they have caught? And none the less are they not slaves. What again? Are not the judges permitted to assess penalties of bondage and death and whatever else they wish against many of those on trial? And surely these are not slaves. And if for the one day on which each is on trial—that is nothing; for indeed a man is already said to become a slave for a single day.

13. But surely, summing up in a word, one must declare that whoever is permitted to do what he wishes is free, and whoever is not permitted, a slave. You will not, then, say this of those at sea, nor of the sick, nor of soldiers, nor of those learning letters or to play the cithara or to wrestle or some other craft; for these are not permitted to act as they themselves wish, but as the steersman and physician and teacher prescribe. Nor, then, are the rest permitted to do what they wish; but if a man acts contrary to the established laws, he will be punished.

14. Then whatever is neither forbidden by the laws nor commanded—the man who has, in these matters, the power himself of acting as he wishes is free, but the man who, on the contrary, is unable, a slave. What then? Do you think you are permitted to do whatever is not forbidden by the laws in writing, but otherwise seems shameful to men and out of place?—I mean, for instance, to be a tax-farmer or a keeper of a brothel or to do other such things? No, by Zeus, I should say that such things too are not permitted to the free. For concerning these too there lies a penalty—to be hated or held in disgust by men.

15. What again? For licentious men, all that they do through licentiousness, and for the senseless, all that they do through folly, whether neglecting their substance or their body, or behaving unjustly and senselessly toward one another—are not all these things penal to those who do them? For they are harmed either in the body or the substance or, what is greatest, in their own soul.—That is true.—Then neither are these things permitted to do?—They are not.

16. In a word, then, must we say that the base and out-of-place and disadvantageous things are not permitted to do, but the just and advantageous and good things befit a man and are permitted?—So it seems to me, at least.—Then to no one is it without penalty to do the base and disadvantageous things, neither to Greek nor barbarian, nor to one for whom a man has given silver as his price?—Certainly not.—But the opposite things are alike allowed to all, and those who do the things allowed continue without penalty, while those who do the things forbidden are penalized.

17. Do others, then, seem to you to do the things permitted than those who understand them, and others the opposite than those who are ignorant?—By no means.—Then the prudent are permitted to do whatever they wish; but the senseless attempt to do what they wish though it is not permitted; so that it must be that the prudent are free and are permitted to do as they wish, while the senseless are slaves and do the things not permitted to them?—Perhaps.

18. Then we must call freedom the knowledge of what is allowed and what forbidden, and slavery the ignorance of what is permitted and what not. And by this argument nothing would prevent the Great King, wearing a very great tiara upon his head, from being a slave and from being permitted to do nothing of what he does; for he will do everything penally and disadvantageously. And some other man, reputed and named a slave—not once, but many times, should it so chance, sold, and, if it so happen, wearing very heavy fetters—would be more free than the Great King.

19. To me it seems very strange, if a man wearing fetters or branded or grinding in a mill shall be more free than the Great King.—What then? Have you been in Thrace?—I have.—Have you, then, seen there the free women full of brands, and having so many more brands and more varied the better and of better stock they are reputed?—What of that?—That a queen, it seems, nothing prevents from being branded; but a king, do you think, is prevented?

20. You, then, have not even heard of that nation among whom the king is guarded in a very lofty tower, and it is not permitted him to come down from the tower? But if you had heard, you would have known that even a king may be one shut in. And perhaps you would hear those men marvelling, if you should recount to them about the king of the Persians, and disbelieving that there is a king who drives about on a chariot and goes wherever he wishes.—But you will not prove that a king is bound.

21. Not, perhaps, among men; since the king of the gods, the first and eldest, is bound, as they say—if one must believe Hesiod and Homer and other wise men, who say these things about Cronus—and, by Zeus, not having suffered this unjustly at the hands of an enemy, but at the hands of the most just and most dear, plainly because that one did it as a kingly thing and advantageous to him.

22. But men are ignorant of this, and would never suppose that a beggar or a prisoner or a man without repute had become a king—although they hear of Odysseus, that being a beggar and asking alms of the suitors he was none the less a king and lord of the house; whereas Antinous and Eurymachus, whom Homer called kings, were wretched and ill-fated. But these things, as I said, they are ignorant of; and they put round their kings as signs tiaras and scepters and diadems, that they may not escape notice in being kings—just as, I think, masters put marks upon their cattle, that they may be recognized.

23. And so the king of the Persians took thought how he alone should wear the tiara upright, and if any other man did this, he straightway bade him be put to death, as though it were not seemly nor advantageous, among so many tens of thousands of men, that two should be wearing their tiaras upright; but how he should keep his judgment upright, and that no one else should be wiser than he in thought, he cared nothing at all.

24. Let it not be, then, that, just as of the kingship of that time such were the signs, so now too freedom must have such tokens, and a man must walk about with a felt cap upon his head, and that otherwise we shall not be able to recognize the free man from the slave.
